text: Every dialect needs to page through results, but the syntax for it varies more than almost anything else in SQL. In this lesson we'll compare SQL Server's TOP, Oracle's ROWNUM and FETCH FIRST, and MySQL and PostgreSQL's LIMIT, including a real trap that catches people switching into Oracle.

SQL Server's TOP ten, order by list price descending, is the simplest limiter — but notice it only limits, it doesn't skip. To get page two, you need the standard OFFSET ten rows, fetch next ten rows only, which SQL Server has supported since the 2012 release. TOP alone has no concept of skipping rows at all.

Here's the classic Oracle trap. Where ROWNUM is less than or equal to ten, order by list price descending, looks reasonable, but it's wrong. ROWNUM gets assigned as rows come out of the table scan, in whatever order the optimizer happens to produce — and that filter runs before ORDER BY ever sorts anything. You get ten arbitrary rows, sorted after the fact, not the ten most expensive products.

The fix is to sort first, inside a subquery, and only then apply ROWNUM to the already-ordered result — that way the numbering happens after the sort, not before it. Oracle twelve c and later also gives you the ANSI-standard fetch first ten rows only, which sidesteps the ROWNUM trap completely and reads almost like the SQL Server version.

MySQL and PostgreSQL both use limit ten offset ten — simple, and nearly identical across both platforms. PostgreSQL is flexible enough to also accept the ANSI offset-fetch form if you prefer consistency with SQL Server and Oracle twelve c code.

So: TOP limits but can't skip, ROWNUM gets assigned before sorting unless you force the order first, and LIMIT-OFFSET is MySQL and PostgreSQL's native shorthand for the same idea. Next up: string concatenation, where plus, double-pipe, and CONCAT each mean something different depending on the platform you're on.
